## The assignment

In class we built a house price model for Philadelphia. Now your team does it for a city you haven't modeled: **Chicago**.

The Cook County Assessor's Office has to value every home in the county, including the vast majority that didn't sell this year. Assessments drive property tax bills. When they're wrong in a systematic way, some households pay more than their share. A 2017 *Chicago Tribune* investigation, "The Tax Divide," found exactly that in Cook County: lower-value homes were assessed at higher shares of their worth than expensive ones.

Build a model that predicts **single-family sale prices in Chicago, 2023–2025**, using only the tools from this course. The file contains **only features of the house itself**. Everything about location is yours to build.

### A real test

| File | What's in it |
|---|---|
| `chicago_train.csv` | About 80% of the houses, **with** sale prices |
| `chicago_test.csv` | The other 20%, **without** sale prices. You predict them; we score you. |

The test houses were held out by house, not by sale, so a house that sold twice is entirely on one side. Your CV RMSE is your estimate. Your test RMSE is the truth. **If they're far apart, something leaked.** 

**Due:** Friday, October 30. All teammates renders the file on their portfolio and every member submits that link on Canvas. One teammate uploads `team_XX_predictions.csv`.

**Individual accountability:** Q7 on October 30 asks each of you about *this* model: which features you used and why, your CV and test RMSE, and where the model fails worst. Make sure everyone can explain all of it.

### Rules

::: {.callout-important}
## 1. Clean training rows once, in Part 1. Never drop test rows.
You must predict every test house, so fill NAs in a feature rather than filtering.

## 2. Stay inside the time window
Open data from 2023–2025 only.

## 3. No leakage
Nothing built from sale prices. *Would the Assessor have this number for a house that didn't sell?*

## 4. The outcome stays in dollars
Transform predictors, not `sale_price`.

## 5. No prices from the test fold or the future
No features built from other houses' sale prices. 
:::

### Please include in your final rendered qmd for this assignment:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Model log** | Every model you tried, in order, with CV RMSE and Moran's I. Each row has a note saying why you tried it. |
| **Features** | Incorporate the feature engineering tricks - including the spatial ones covered these past few weeks. 
| **Diagnostics** | Residual maps for your baseline and final model, and what changed. |
| **Error analysis** | Where your final model fails worst, and whose homes it over-values (Part 4). |
| **Reasoning** | Choices justified by evidence from your own analysis.

## Part 0: Setup (provided)

These helpers are to help you get off the ground.


::: {.cell}

:::

```{.r .cell-code}
check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")
  }
}

# 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

# Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out
cv_pred <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))
  url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q)
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url)
  st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE)
}
```

## Part 2: Build the model

Start with a structure-only baseline. Then add features in steps you can learn from, logging each one. Keep the log in a tibble with columns `model`, `added`, `cv_rmse`, `moran_i`, `notes`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#baseline
m1 <- lm(sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + lotsize_acre, data = train)
#summary(m1)

#added
m2 <- lm(sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + lotsize_acre +num_bedrooms +num_fireplaces, data = train)

#log version
m_log <- lm(sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + lotsize_acre + log1p(num_bedrooms) + num_fireplaces, data = train)

rmse1 <- cv_rmse(formula(m1), train)
rmse2 <- cv_rmse(formula(m2), train)
rmse3 <- cv_rmse(formula(m_log), train)

coords <- as.matrix(train[, c("lon", "lat")])
nb <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 5))
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W")

mi1 <- moran.mc(residuals(m1), lw, nsim = 999)   
mi2 <- moran.mc(residuals(m2), lw, nsim = 999) 
mi3 <- moran.mc(residuals(m_log), lw, nsim = 999)
  
tibb <- tibble(
  model   = c("m1", "m2", "m_log"),
  added   = c("Structure-only baseline", "Bedrooms + fireplaces", "Logged features"),
  cv_rmse = c(rmse1, rmse2, rmse3),
  moran_i = c(mi1$statistic, mi2$statistic, mi3$statistic),
  notes   = c("features that didn't need as much cleaning", "added bedroooms and fireplace for details aside from size", "logged bedrooms so each extra bedroom doesn't add more than the one before")
)
```

**Answer:** What helped most, and what disappointed you? Use your log.

*Your answer:*
The feature engineering that assisted the model most was adding more features, especially logging the number of bedrooms. Logging more than the selected features actually increased the RMSE in my model so I removed that. The biggest disappointment was our moran's i results. The baseline outperformed the other models in terms of spatial correlation but not by much, 0.01. 

The baseline and final residual maps are nearly identical. There was underprediction in both for a large cluster in the north and overprediction across much of the south. Adding bedrooms and fireplaces changed how individual houses were priced but not where the model was wrong. The Morans I didn't seem to move much and our model doesn't contain neighborhood information. 

---

## Part 4: Where it fails, and who pays

**4A.** Where does your final model fail worst? Is it guessing too high or too low there, and why do you think so?

The model fails the worst in the north because it is guessing too low when it only knows few details such as the house's size,lot, age, and rooms. Homes in high-demand neighborhoods are likely under-valued while the model over-predicts in the south. 

**4B.** Assessors judge their work with the **ratio** of predicted value to sale price. A ratio above 1 means the home is over-valued and its owner over-taxed. Does your model's ratio differ by neighborhood income? Connect your answer to your Part 1 cleaning rules and to "The Tax Divide."

Yes, in ours, regressing each tract’s log median ratio on its poverty rate gives a coefficient of 0.026, p < 0.001 and R² = 0.36. Each one-point rise in poverty raises the median ratio by about 2.6%. At about 16% poverty, the ratio crosses 1 and reaches about 1.42 at 30% poverty.

“The Tax Divide” exists because lower-value homes are assessed at higher shares of their worth. Our model has no location features, so it pulls predictions toward the average. This results in pushing cheap homes up and expensive ones down. Dropping sales over $1 million in Part 1 removed the top of the price range and strengthened that pull.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

m_final <- lm(f_final, data = st_drop_geometry(train))
```

## Part 6: Reflection (about 300 words, as a team)

1. **Read one coefficient twice:** once as β̂, once for what it does to ŷ.
2. **Would you hand this model to the Assessor?** What would you warn them about?

Our final model enters bedrooms as log1p(num_bedrooms). As β̂, the coefficient of −53,611 is the change in predicted sale price for a one-unit increase in log(1 + bedrooms), holding living area, age, lot size, and fireplaces fixed. This is admittedly hard to navigate as one rarely adds “one log unit” of bedrooms to a house.

With ŷ, going from 2 to 3 bedrooms raises log1p by log(4/3) ≈ 0.29, so ŷ drops by about \$15,400. Going from 4 to 5 adds only log(6/5) ≈ 0.18, so ŷ drops by about \$9,800 and an added bedroom matters less than the one before. Since living area is held fixed, the negative coefficient means that dividing the same square footage into more, smaller rooms lowers predicted price.

We would not submit to an assessor just yet, as the model knows what a house is but not where it is. Our residual maps show clustering of underprediction and overprediction in different parts of the city, and the baseline and final maps look nearly identical.  Moran’s I barely changed, so the features we added don't address our errors as well as we want them to.

We would warn the assessor about the "Tax Divide" where a model built only on structure pulls predictions toward the average. This would bring cheap homes up and expensive ones down. Dropping sales over $1 million narrowed what the model learned from and strengthened that pull. In our results, the ratio rises about 2.6% with every point of tract poverty. We are at 1 at about 16% poverty and about 1.42 at 30%. This would mean that an assessor mistakingly sends relative tax bills to households with less means to pay them.

For future adjustments, we would add location features (such as Census tract data) and then check whether the ratio still rises with poverty.
